[[File:San_Bernardino_County_California_Incorporated_and_Unincorporated_areas_Adelanto_Highlighted.svg|thumb|Location of Adelanto in San Bernardino County, and San Bernardino County in California]]

The '''Adelanto ICE detention facilities''' are a privately operated [[Immigration detention in the United States#Detention centers|immigration detention center]]<ref>{{cite news|title=Second ICE Detainee at Adelanto Detention Center Dies in as Many Weeks|url=http://ktla.com/2017/04/14/second-ice-detainee-at-adelanto-detention-center-dies-in-as-many-weeks/|work=KTLA|date=14 April 2017}}</ref> in [[Adelanto, California|Adelanto]], [[San Bernardino County, California]].  Operated by the [[GEO Group]], they comprise a cluster of three adjacent facilities. Adelanto East was an existing prison that was purchased in June 2010 from the City of Adelanto, with a capacity of about 600 inmates; the newly built Adelanto West facility was completed in August 2012, with another 700 beds.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.geogroup.com/maps/locationdetails/35 |title=Adelanto Detention Facility |publisher =The GEO Group Inc  |date=2011-05-27 |accessdate=2016-05-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160506193419/http://www.geogroup.com/maps/locationdetails/35 |archive-date=2016-05-06 |url-status=dead }}</ref> After an additional expansion in 2015, the facility can accommodate up to 1,940 immigrant detainees of all classification levels, with an average stay of 30 days.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.scpr.org/programs/take-two/2016/10/11/51552/inside-the-adelanto-detention-facility-troubled-hi/ | title=Inside the Adelanto detention facility: Troubled history, vows for reform | date=11 October 2016 }}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.oig.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/assets/2018-10/OIG-18-86-Sep18.pdf|title=DHS OIG HIGHLIGHTS: Management Alert – Issues Requiring Action at the Adelanto ICE Processing Center in Adelanto, California|date=September 27, 2018|website=www.oig.dhs.gov|access-date=2018-12-14}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ice.gov/doclib/foia/odo-compliance-inspections/adelantoCorrectionalFac_Adelanto-CA-Sept_18-20-2012.pdf|title=Office of Detention Oversight Compliance Inspection|date=September 18–20, 2012|website=www.ice.gov|access-date=2018-12-14}}</ref>

== History ==
From 1991 Adelanto was a state prison for adult male inmates. The GEO Group purchased the facility in 2010 and in May 2011, contracted with the [[U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement]] (ICE) to house federal immigration detainees.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://m.ice.gov/detention-facilities/facilities/adlntca.htm |title=Adelanto Detention Facility |accessdate=March 3, 2014 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140303045514/http://m.ice.gov/detention-facilities/facilities/adlntca.htm |archivedate=March 3, 2014 }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2018/10/03/politics/immigrant-detention-adelanto-oig-report/index.html|title=Inspectors found nooses hanging in cells at an ICE detention facility|last=Shoichet|first=Catherine E.|date=October 3, 2018|work=CNN|access-date=14 December 2018}}</ref> Based on the agreement, the center must comply with ICE’s 2011 Performance-Based National Detention Standards, which establish requirements for environmental health and safety, detainee care, activities, and grievance system.<ref name=":0" /> The GEO Group also receives a fee of up to about $112 per day per detainee from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, with the city of Adelanto serving as a go-between.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.latimes.com/local/lanow/la-me-ln-adelanto-detention-20170808-story.html|title='We don't feel OK here': Detainee deaths, suicide attempts and hunger strikes plague California immigration facility|date=August 8, 2017|newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]]|last=Esquivel|first=Paloma|access-date=2018-12-14}}</ref> This used a complicated subcontracting model so ICE and Adelanto didn't need to award the contract for the center’s operations using competitive bidding as required under  Federal regulations.<ref name="Gu 2019-09-12">{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2019/sep/12/california-private-prison-ban-immigration-ice|title=California bans private prisons – including Ice detention centers|last=BondGraham|first=Darwin|date=2019-09-12|work=The Guardian|access-date=2019-09-13|language=en-GB|issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

In 2016, the city of Adelanto extended the company’s contract until 2021.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news|url=https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2017/06/adelanto-death-immigration-detention-geo/|title=In 3 months, 3 immigrants have died at this private detention center|work=Mother Jones|language=en-US|access-date=2018-12-14|last=Pauly|first=Madison|date=June 2, 2017}}</ref> The Department of Homeland Security purchased the three facilities in 2026 while GEO will continue to manage them under the existing contract through Dec. 19, 2034.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Castillo |first=Andrea |date=2026-10-05 |title=DHS buys three detention centers in California for $950 million |url=https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-10-05/dhs-buys-three-detention-centers-in-california-for-950-million |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}}</ref>

{{Bar chart|title=Average daily population at Adelanto ICE Processing Center<ref name="ice-detention-fy19-fy26">{{Cite web | publisher = U.S. Department of Homeland Security | last = U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement | title = ICE Detention Statistics FY 2019 | date = 2019-09-30 | url = https://www.ice.gov/doclib/detention/FY19-detentionstats.xlsx}} Additional fiscal year data: [https://www.ice.gov/doclib/detention/FY20-detentionstats.xlsx FY20], [https://www.ice.gov/doclib/detention/FY21-detentionstats.xlsx FY21], [https://www.ice.gov/doclib/detention/FY22-detentionStats.xlsx FY22], [https://www.ice.gov/doclib/detention/FY23_detentionStats.xlsx FY23], [https://www.ice.gov/doclib/detention/FY24_detentionStats.xlsx FY24], [https://www.ice.gov/doclib/detention/FY25_detentionStats09242025.xlsx FY25], [https://www.ice.gov/doclib/detention/FY26_detentionStats02022026.xlsx FY26].</ref><ref name="ice-dmcp-faclist17">{{Cite web | publisher = U.S. Department of Homeland Security | last = U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement | title = ICE DMCP Facility List — ERO Custody Management Division, FY2017 | date = 2017-07-10 | url = https://www.prisonlegalnews.org/media/publications/ICE_DMCP_Facility_List_ERO_Custody_Management_Division_2017.pdf}}</ref>|bar_width=35|data_max=2,329|label_type=Fiscal year|data_type=ADP|label1=FY 2011|data1=19|label2=FY 2012|data2=587|label3=FY 2013|data3=1,081|label4=FY 2014|data4=1,209|label5=FY 2015|data5=1,180|label6=FY 2016|data6=1,472|label7=FY 2017|data7=1,745|label8=FY 2019|data8=1,711|label9=FY 2020|data9=1,291|label10=FY 2021|data10=276|label11=FY 2022|data11=138|label12=FY 2023|data12=219|label13=FY 2024|data13=396|label14=FY 2025|data14=999|label15=FY 2026|data15=2,218}}

== Conditions ==
The prison, then ICE's newest and largest in California,<ref>{{cite news|url=http://lens.blogs.nytimes.com/2013/11/25/an-immigrants-dream-detained/?_php=true&_type=blogs&_r=0|title=An Immigrant's Dream, Detained|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=25 November 2013 |accessdate=3 May 2016}}</ref> was the scene of small immigration protests in November 2013.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sbsun.com/general-news/20131125/protesters-decry-unjust-treatment-at-adelanto-detention-facility |title=Protesters decry 'unjust' treatment at Adelanto detention facility |publisher=Sbsun.com |date=2013-11-25 |accessdate=2016-05-03}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://blog.pe.com/multicultural-empire/2013/11/25/adelanto-protest-at-immigration-detention-center/ |title=ADELANTO: Protest at immigration detention center |accessdate=March 3, 2014 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140303035526/http://blog.pe.com/multicultural-empire/2013/11/25/adelanto-protest-at-immigration-detention-center/ |archivedate=March 3, 2014 }}</ref>

Since its opening as an ICE detention center in 2011, Adelanto Detention Facility has faced accusations of insufficient medical care and poor conditions. Because of the poor conditions, in July 2015, 29 members of Congress sent a letter to ICE and federal inspectors requesting an investigation addressing their concerns. Later that year in November, 400 detainees went on a hunger strike, to demand better medical and dental care.<ref name=":2" />

In May 2018, government inspectors from the [[United States Department of Homeland Security|Department of Homeland Security]] (DHS) made a surprise visit to the detention center where 307 contract guards oversaw 1,659 immigrant detainees housed in different facilities around the center. Inspectors found multiple violations of ICE detention standards which posed significant health and safety risks for detainees and restricted detainees' rights. The violations found were: nooses in detainee cells, inappropriate segregation including misuse of solitary confinement, improperly handcuffed and shackled, and detainees with limited English lacked communication assistance; and untimely and inadequate detainee medical care.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" />

During the [[COVID-19 pandemic in the United States|COVID-19 pandemic]], a lawsuit was filed on behalf of six detainees with medical conditions due to inadequate sanitation and beds placed too close together. These conditions provided an “ideal incubation” opportunity for coronavirus.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ocregister.com/coronavirus-lawsuit-conditions-for-immigrant-detainees-in-adelanto-ideal-for-disease|title=Coronavirus lawsuit: Conditions for immigrant detainees in Adelanto 'ideal' for disease|date=2020-03-31|website=Orange County Register|language=en-US|access-date=2020-03-31}}</ref>

== ''Hernandez v. Sessions'' ==
''Hernandez v. Sessions'' is a class action lawsuit filed in April 2016 by the [[American Civil Liberties Union|ACLU]] and pro bono lawyers from [[Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom]]. Lead plaintiffs in the case were non-citizens who were detained at Adelanto Detention Facility due to their inability to afford the bond set by immigration officials. In October 2017, the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit|U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit]] affirmed a district court’s order granting a classwide preliminary injunction in favor the plaintiffs. The ''Hernandez'' decision is the first court case to impose due process requirements in the immigration context and requires ICE officers and immigration judges to consider a person's financial ability to post bond and suitability for non-monetary alternative conditions of supervision when considering the conditions of release.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.law.com/nationallawjournal/2018/04/30/ninth-circuit-win-garners-bail-hearings-for-immigrant-detainees/|title=Fighting for Bond Hearings for Detainees|last1=April 30|first1=Rich Acello {{!}}|last2=AM|first2=2018 at 02:00|website=National Law Journal|access-date=2018-12-14}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aclu.org/other/practice-advisory-bond-hearing-and-ability-pay-determinations|title=Practice Advisory: Bond Hearing and Ability-to-Pay Determinations|website=American Civil Liberties Union|language=en|access-date=2018-12-14}}</ref>
